title: BiBi-Linux_Wiper_Incident_Response_b5a
description: Investigate and respond to a BiBi-Linux Wiper malware incident on a corporate network.

levels.title: Introduction
levels.content: The corporate network has experienced a security incident involving data destruction caused by the BiBi-Linux Wiper malware. As an incident responder, your task is to investigate the affected systems, identify the cause of the incident, and contain the threat.

levels.title: Get Access
levels.cloud_content: You have SSH access to the workstation (192.168.50.5) as user 'cyrano' with password 'cyrano'. From there, you can investigate the system and access other network resources as needed. Enter the word 'start' to proceed to the next level.
levels.local_content: You have SSH access to the workstation (192.168.50.5) as user 'cyrano' with password 'cyrano'. From there, you can investigate the system and access other network resources as needed. Enter the word 'start' to proceed to the next level.

levels.title: Identify Evidence of File Destruction
levels.content: Investigate the workstation for signs of file destruction. Look for unusual file modifications, missing files, or other indicators that files have been intentionally destroyed.
levels.solution: Check the contents of the /data/company_files directory and look for unusual file names or modifications. The malware renames files to random hex strings. Use the command 'ls -la /data/company_files' to list the files and identify the randomly renamed file, such as 'a1b2c3d4e5f6.txt'.

hints.title: Conceptual Hint
hints.content: Consider how a wiper malware like BiBi-Linux might alter file names to hide its activity.

hints.title: Directional Hint
hints.content: Examine the /data/company_files directory for any unusual file names, particularly those resembling random hex strings.

hints.title: Near-Spoiler Hint
hints.content: The malware renames files to random hex strings in the /data/company_files directory, such as 'a1b2c3d4e5f6.txt'.

levels.title: Locate the Malware Binary
levels.content: Search the workstation for suspicious executables or binaries that might be responsible for the file destruction. Pay attention to unusual file locations, permissions, or timestamps.
levels.solution: Check the /usr/local/sbin directory for suspicious files. The malware binary is named 'disk-maintenance'. Use the command 'ls -la /usr/local/sbin' to list the files and identify the malware binary 'disk-maintenance'.

hints.title: Conceptual Hint
hints.content: Think about where malware authors might place their binaries to avoid detection, such as in system directories.

hints.title: Directional Hint
hints.content: Investigate the /usr/local/sbin directory for any suspicious files, particularly those with unusual names.

hints.title: Near-Spoiler Hint
hints.content: The malware binary is named 'disk-maintenance' and is located in the /usr/local/sbin directory.

levels.title: Determine Persistence Mechanism
levels.content: Investigate the workstation for persistence mechanisms that might be used to automatically execute the malware. Look for scheduled tasks, services, or other methods of ensuring the malware runs automatically.
levels.solution: Check the contents of the /etc/systemd/system directory for suspicious service or timer files. The malware uses a systemd service named 'disk-maintenance.service' and a timer named 'disk-maintenance.timer'. Use the command 'ls -la /etc/systemd/system' to list the files and identify the persistence mechanism 'disk-maintenance.service'.

hints.title: Conceptual Hint
hints.content: Consider how malware might ensure it runs automatically after a system reboot, such as by using system services.

hints.title: Directional Hint
hints.content: Examine the /etc/systemd/system directory for any suspicious service or timer files, particularly those related to disk maintenance.

hints.title: Near-Spoiler Hint
hints.content: The malware uses a systemd service named 'disk-maintenance.service' and a timer named 'disk-maintenance.timer' in the /etc/systemd/system directory.
